title: Sciatica
description: Lower-back pain that can extend down the leg
wiki_lead:
Sciatica is pain going down the leg from the lower back. This pain may extend down the back, outside, or front of the leg. The onset is often sudden following activities such as heavy lifting, although it may also occur gradually. The pain is often described as shooting. Typically, symptoms occur on only one side of the body; certain causes, however, may result in pain on both sides. Lower back pain is sometimes present. Weakness or numbness may occur in different parts of the affected leg and foot.
About 90% of sciatica is due to a spinal disc herniation pressing on one of the lumbar or sacral nerve roots. Spondylolisthesis, spinal stenosis, piriformis syndrome, pelvic tumors, and pregnancy are other possible causes of sciatica. The straight-leg-raising test is often helpful in diagnosis. The test is positive if, when the leg is raised while a person is lying on their back, pain shoots below the knee. In most cases medical imaging is not needed. However, imaging may be obtained if bowel or bladder function is affected, there is significant loss of feeling or weakness, symptoms are long standing, or there is a concern for tumor or infection. Conditions that can present similarly are diseases of the hip and infections such as early shingles (prior to rash formation).
Initial treatment typically consists of pain medications. However, evidence for effectiveness of pain medication, and of muscle relaxants, is lacking. It is generally recommended that people continue with normal activity to the best of their abilities. Often all that is required for resolution of sciatica is time; in about 90% of cases, symptoms resolve in less than six weeks. If the pain is severe and lasts for more than six weeks, surgery may be an option. While surgery often speeds pain improvement, its long term benefits are unclear. Surgery may be required if complications occur, such as loss of normal bowel or bladder function. Many treatments, including corticosteroids, gabapentin, pregabalin, acupuncture, heat or ice, and spinal manipulation, have only limited or poor evidence supporting their use.
Depending on how it is defined, less than 1% to 40% of people have sciatica at some point in time. Sciatica is most common between the ages of 40 and 59, and men are more frequently affected than women. The condition has been known since ancient times. The first known modern use of the word sciatica dates from 1451, although Dioscorides (1st-century CE) mentions it in his Materia Medica.

Definition

The term "sciatica" usually describes a symptom—pain along the sciatic nerve pathway—rather than a specific condition, illness, or disease. Some use it to mean any pain starting in the lower back and going down the leg. The pain is characteristically described as shooting or shock-like, quickly traveling along the course of the affected nerves. grok_lead: Sciatica is pain that radiates along the path of the sciatic nerve, the longest and widest nerve in the human body, which originates from nerve roots in the lower ( lumbar) spine (L4 to S3), travels through the pelvis and buttocks, and extends down the back of each leg to the foot. Typically affecting only one side of the body, it manifests as a symptom rather than a standalone condition, often resulting from compression, irritation, or inflammation of the sciatic nerve or its contributing spinal nerve roots. The condition can range from mild discomfort to severe, debilitating pain, with symptoms worsening during activities like coughing, sneezing, or prolonged sitting. Common symptoms include sharp, burning, or electric-shock-like pain starting in the lower back or buttock and extending to the thigh, calf, or foot, often accompanied by numbness, tingling ( paresthesia), or muscle weakness in the affected leg. In severe cases, it may cause difficulty controlling the leg muscles, leading to foot drop, or loss of bowel/bladder control, which requires immediate medical attention as it could indicate cauda equina syndrome. The sciatic nerve provides motor control to the muscles in the back of the knee and lower leg while supplying sensation to the back of the thigh, lower leg, and sole of the foot. The primary cause of sciatica is a herniated or bulging lumbar disk that presses on a nerve root, accounting for about 90% of cases, though other etiologies include spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis, bone spurs (osteophytes), piriformis syndrome, or rarely, tumors, abscesses, or hematomas. Pathophysiology often involves both mechanical compression and inflammatory responses around the nerve, contributing to the pain. Risk factors encompass age (peaking in the 20sâ50s due to disk issues, or later for degenerative changes), obesity, diabetes (which affects nerve health), occupations involving heavy lifting, twisting, or prolonged sitting (e.g., truck drivers or machine operators), sedentary lifestyles, and dehydration. Dehydration can worsen sciatica and the associated electric shock-like pain by dehydrating spinal discs, causing them to lose fluid, shrink, become less flexible, and reduce cushioning between vertebrae. This increases pressure on the sciatic nerve, leading to intensified pain, numbness, tingling, and radiating electric shock sensations. Dehydration also promotes muscle tightening, spasms, reduced circulation, and inflammation, further irritating the nerve. Epidemiologically, sciatica has a lifetime prevalence of 10%â40% and an annual incidence of 1%â5%, with no significant gender difference and rare occurrence before age 20 absent trauma. Most cases resolve spontaneously within weeks to months through conservative management, including pain relievers, physical therapy, and lifestyle modifications, though persistent or severe symptoms may necessitate epidural steroid injections or surgery like microdiscectomy. Diagnosis typically involves a physical exam, imaging (MRI or CT), and ruling out differentials like peripheral neuropathy or vascular issues.
